match.reason: The closest bank point, Comparing ratios, covers comparing with past results, similar businesses and targets, but it omits the new point's central limit that methods, timing and one-off events restrict what a comparison shows, so adapting it would need a new idea rather than a small change.

draft.title: Comparing performance
card: A ratio on its own says little. A net profit margin of 8% is neither good nor bad until it is compared with something.
Three useful comparisons are past results of the same business, the budget (what the business planned), and similar businesses in the same industry.

Comparisons can mislead if businesses use different methods, such as different depreciation or inventory methods. They can also mislead if the periods differ, such as a seasonal peak against a quiet season.
A one-off event, such as the sale of a building at a large gain, can distort one year's result. It does not show how the business normally performs.
draft.remember: A ratio means most when compared, but methods, timing and one-off events can distort the comparison.

a.q: Kim's shop has a net profit margin of 8% this year. Which comparison would best help Kim judge whether 8% is a good result?
opts: The shop's margin in earlier years and the industry's margin
The shop's margin and its total assets this year
The shop's margin and the number of staff it employs
The shop's margin this year and its closing cash balance
a.why: A ratio only has meaning when set against past results, the budget or similar businesses. The other options pair the ratio with a figure from the same year that gives no standard to judge it against.
a.clue: Compare the ratio with a standard, not with another figure from this year.

b.q: Two bakeries in Ballarat have the same gross profit margin. Bakery A sold a delivery van this year at a large gain, which is included in its net profit. Why is comparing their net profit margins unreliable?
opts: The one-off gain on the van inflates Bakery A's net profit
Bakeries with equal gross margins must have equal net profit
The budget is not needed when comparing two businesses
Net profit margins can only be compared within one business
b.why: The gain on the van is a one-off event, so it lifts Bakery A's net profit for this year only and does not show its normal performance. The last option is wrong because comparing with similar businesses is useful, as long as the differences are allowed for.
b.clue: Ask whether the van sale will happen again next year.

a.best: The shop's margin in earlier years and the industry's margin

b.best: The one-off gain on the van inflates Bakery A's net profit

problems.detail: Two distractors use absolutes ('must have equal net profit', 'can only be compared'), while the card says comparisons 'can' mislead. A student can rule these out without knowing the idea.
Why (a) says a ratio 'only has meaning' when compared. The card says more softly that a ratio on its own 'says little'.

The clue says not to compare 'with another figure from this year', yet the right option includes the industry's margin, which is also a figure from this year. It should say another of the shop's own figures from this year.
